paragraphs.source_en: I think this is quite enough by way of explaining the rush of blood to the head; from here I shall finally take up the matter itself. However, before any great incident occurs, certain minor incidents are bound to occur first. To describe only the great events and let the small ones slip away is a failing into which historians have always fallen. My master's rush of blood, too, grew more violent with every minor incident it encountered, until at last it brought about the great incident. For that reason, unless I set out its development in proper order, it will be hard to understand just how my master came to be so overwrought. If it is not thoroughly understood, my master's rush of blood will amount to an empty name, and society may look down on him, thinking it surely cannot have reached the proper degree. After going to the trouble of such a rush of blood, would it not be disheartening if people failed to praise it as a truly splendid one? The events I am about to relate, great or small, are not exactly honorable ones for my master. Since the events themselves are hardly honorable, I should at least like to make clear, on the point of his rush of blood, that it was a genuine article and by no means inferior to anyone else's. My master does not possess any particular quality that he can boast of to others. Unless I show off even his rush of blood, there is nothing else worth the trouble of writing up for him.

paragraphs.source_zh: 关于虚火上升的解释，我想这已满够了，下边就要谈事件的正题了。不过，任何一桩大事件发生之前，总要发生一些小事件的。只叙述大事件而漏掉小事件是历来历史学家常有的弊端。主人的虚火上升也是每碰上一次小事件就上升一层，终于惹出了大事件。基于这个道理，如果我不把它的发展过程条理清晰地叙述出来，那么就不容易了解主人是怎样虚火上升的。了解得不彻底，主人的虚火上升就会空有虚名，社会上也许会瞧不起主人，认为他的虚火上升还未达到应有的程度。难得有这么一次虚火上升，如果不被人们推崇是一次十分了不起的虚火上升，岂不是让人泄气吗？下边叙述的事件，不论大小，对主人来说都不见得是光荣的。事件本身既然谈不上光荣，那么起码在虚火上升这一点上，最好能充分证明这是货真价实的虚火上升，是不比别人落后的虚火上升。我的主人并不具备向他人夸示什么的性格。如果不把他的虚火上升拿来炫耀一番，那就没有值得我费力去写的东西了。

paragraphs.source_en: The enemy forces gathered at Rakun-kan have recently invented a kind of dum-dum bullet, and during each ten-minute recess or after classes they pour fire toward the vacant lot on the north side. This dum-dum bullet is commonly called a ball, and the apparatus for firing it is a large implement something like a kitchen pestle, by which it is launched at will into the enemy camp. Dum-dum bullet though it may be, since it is fired from the Rakun-kan athletic field, there is no need to worry that it will strike my master, who is barricaded all day in his study. Even the enemy cannot fail to realize that the trajectory is much too long, but therein lies their strategy: if, as they say, the navy achieved great success at Port Arthur by indirect fire, then even balls rolling into the vacant lot may well produce some result. All the more so when, with every shot they send forth, the whole army combines its strength to emit a threatening roar of “Waa!” As a result of his alarm, the blood vessels running through my master's limbs cannot help contracting; at the height of his vexation, the blood wandering helplessly about his whole body is bound to rush upward. One may say that the enemy's stratagem is remarkably clever. They say that in ancient Greece there was a writer named Aeschylus, and that this man had the sort of head common to scholars and writers. By the head common to scholars and writers, I mean a bald head. Why do people's heads go bald? It is no doubt because, through lack of nourishment, the hair has lost the vigor to grow. Scholars and writers use their heads more than anyone, and they are generally desperately poor besides. Therefore the heads of scholars and writers are, without exception, bare and shiny. Now Aeschylus too was a writer, so naturally he too had to be bald. He possessed a smooth, glossy, kumquat-like head. One day, however, this gentleman was walking along the street in the sunlight, shaking that ever-familiar bald head of his, a head cannot be bald on some occasions and not bald on others, so one can only call it his ever-familiar bald head. There lay the source of the mistake. When a bald head is exposed to the sun and seen from far away, it gleams exceedingly bright. A tall tree catches the wind. A shining head, of course, must catch something too. At that moment an eagle was circling above Aeschylus's head, and on looking closely, one saw that in its talons it clutched a small tortoise it had apparently just captured. Tortoises and soft-shelled turtles are, to be sure, delicious things. But since the Greek age they have all come equipped with hard shells. However delicious they may be, there is no eating them with the shell still on. There is a famous dish of prawns grilled in their shells, but even today no dish called tortoise stewed in its shell exists, and it certainly did not exist then. Even the seasoned eagle found itself somewhat at a loss over how to deal with this tortoise. Just then, far below in the lower world, there was something that flashed. At that moment the eagle thought its chance had come: if it dropped the tortoise onto that shining thing, the shell would surely smash to pieces.

paragraphs.source_zh: 群集于落云馆的敌军近日发明了一种达姆达姆弹，每当十分钟的课间休息或放学之后就向北边的空地发射炮火。这种达姆达姆弹，一般将它称之为球，用一个大的、类似厨房用的捣棒似的东西作为发射装置，任意向敌阵发射。别看它是达姆达姆弹，由于它是从落云馆运动场发射出来的，所以不必担心它会击中整天蜷伏在书斋里的主人。虽说是敌人，也不能不意识到这弹道是太远了，不过这是一种作战策略，据说在旅顺战斗中海军进行了间接射击从而建立了伟大的功勋，既然是这样，那么滚进空地来的球，也不见得收不到战果。更何况每打出一球，则竭尽全军之力，“哇”的发出一种威吓性的音响。主人遭受惊吓的结果是四肢的血管收缩，当他烦闷至极时，他那全身走投无路的血，必然就上升。可以说敌人的这一计谋是相当巧妙的。据说古时候希腊有个名叫伊斯基拉斯的作家，此人具有与学者、作家相同的脑袋。我这里说的学者、作家共同的脑袋是指秃头。为什么人们的头都会秃呢？无疑是因为营养不良而使头发失去了生长活力的缘故。学者和作家使用头脑最多，而且一般又都是穷得要命的。所以学者、作家的头一概都是光秃秃的。伊斯基拉斯也是一位作家，所以自然也是个秃头。他有着一个光溜溜的、和金桔一样发亮的脑袋。可是有一天，在阳光照射下，这位老兄摇晃着他那一向光秃秃的脑袋——脑袋是不可能时而光秃秃的，时而不秃，因此，只能说它是一向光秃秃的脑袋——走在大街上。差错就出在这里。秃头经日光一照，从远处一看，显得特别锃光发亮！树大招风嘛。他这个锃光发亮的脑袋当然也得招点什么来。这时，在伊斯基拉斯的头上正飞着一只苍鹰，仔细一看，这只苍鹰的爪子正紧紧地抓住一只小乌龟，这大概是它刚刚捕获的。乌龟、甲鱼这类东西味道当然是极好的。可是从希腊时期起，它们都带上一个硬壳儿。不管多么好吃，带着壳儿总是吃不成的。大对虾有一种带皮烤的名菜，但是带壳儿炖乌龟这道菜至今还没有过，肯定当时也是没有过的。即使老练的苍鹰，对于如何处置这乌龟也感到有些棘手。就在这时，在遥远的下界有个发光的东西。这时苍鹰认为机会来啦，它想如果把这个乌龟扔在这个发光的东西上边，那么乌龟的壳儿肯定会摔碎的。
